newsitem.title: UK: Womb may influence IQ, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Womb may influence IQ, study finds.

text.p: Nurture may rival nature in determining intelligence after all, U.S. researchers said on Wednesday.
They took a second look at studies of twins that are said to show genes play a strong role in determining IQ and found the environment of the womb may be just as important.
Bernie Devlin of the University of Pittsburgh's school of medicine and colleagues re-analysed more than 200 studies looking at intelligence in twins and siblings.
Although they did find strong statistical evidence that there is a genetic influence on intelligence, genetics could not account for all the variations in the studies.

Twins have very similar IQs, but the similarities are so strong that there has to be another factor besides genes, Devlin said. This must be the womb, he wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
"The shared maternal environment may explain the striking correlation between the IQs of twins, especially those of adult twins that were reared apart," he wrote.
Twins are important to IQ studies because they share so many of their genes. Identical twins have all the same genes, while fraternal twins are no more closely related than any brother or sister.
Comparing similarities between fraternal twins to similarities between identical twins helps scientists determine how strong genetic factors actually are.

Devlin estimated genes accounted for about 48 percent of intelligence. The rest had to be environment -- and much of that had to come in the womb because of similarities found in twins separated at birth and raised apart.

They said there was much evidence that development in the womb affected intelligence. "There is substantial brain growth in the womb, and the brain has 70 percent of its final mass within a year of birth," they wrote.

"IQ is positively correlated with birth weight even after controlling for gestational age; twins, who usually weigh less than singletons, average four to seven points lower in IQ tests; some dietary supplements can raise IQs; alcohol, drug and cigarette consumption can lower IQs; and lead exchange from mother to foetus may reduce IQ."
Matt McGue, a geneticist and psychologist at the University of Minnesota, said the fates of royal families proved that elite genes were not always passed down from generation to generation.
"High IQ parents aren't guaranteed to produce high IQ kids," McGue said in a telephone interview.

"We have a term for it -- regression towards the mean. You just can't through genetics establish a genetic aristocracy...You can observe it -- family dynasties come and go. They last for a couple of generations and then they go."
McGue noted that Devlin's analysis was statistical, not medical or scientific. "These are statisticians. One would want to be cautious about not over-interpreting," he said.
